item.title: Production Optimization and Functional Characterization of Melanin Produced by Halotolerant Bacillus atrophaeus Isolated from a Hypersaline Environment
item.description:
Abstract
Melanin is a naturally occurring dark biopolymer widely distributed in microorganisms, plants, and animals, known for its remarkable physicochemical properties, including ultraviolet (UV) protection and antioxidant activity. In this study, a halotolerant bacterial isolate obtained from the hypersaline environment of Tuz Lake was identified as Bacillus atrophaeus and evaluated as a novel source of microbial melanin. The strain was cultivated under batch conditions, and melanin production was optimized using a Box–Behnken experimental design to maximize pigment yield. The extracted melanin was comprehensively characterized by solubility analysis, UV–vis spectroscopy, Fourier-transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy, differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), proton nuclear magnetic resonance (1H NMR) spectroscopy, and scanning electron microscopy coupled with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM–EDS). Comparative analyses with commercial synthetic melanin revealed similarities in physicochemical, thermal, morphological, and spectroscopic characteristics, supporting the classification of the extracted material as a DOPA-dependent eumelanin-like pigment. Biological activity assays demonstrated antimicrobial activity with minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) values ranging from 312.50 to 625.00 μg/mL, concentration-dependent antioxidant activity (39.06–625.00 μg/mL) in the DPPH assay, and significant UV-protective effects, while no cytotoxicity was observed up to 250 μg/mL. Biosynthetic pathway analysis, together with the inhibitor response and 1H NMR findings, supported the involvement of a tyrosinase-mediated DOPA pathway in pigment formation with tyrosine and glucose playing important roles in production enhancement. This study identifies halotolerant Bacillus atrophaeus as a promising microbial source of a functionally active DOPA-dependent eumelanin-like pigment with potential pharmaceutical, cosmetic, and biotechnological applications.

item.title: Integrating Immunotherapy with Locoregional Treatment in Hepatocellular Carcinoma: Mechanistic Insights and Emerging Clinical Strategies
item.description:
Abstract
Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the sixth most commonly diagnosed cancer worldwide and the third leading cause of cancer-related mortality. Chronic viral hepatitis and metabolic liver disease are major contributors to its development. Many patients present with intermediate or advanced disease, for which treatment selection depends on tumor burden, vascular involvement, liver function, performance status, and multidisciplinary assessment. This review evaluates clinical evidence for combining locoregional therapies, including transarterial chemoembolization (TACE), hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy (HAIC), thermal ablation, and transarterial radioembolization (TARE), with immune checkpoint inhibitors and antiangiogenic agents. In the phase III LEAP-012 trial, lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab with TACE improved median progression-free survival (PFS) compared with TACE alone (14.6 versus 10.0 months; hazard ratio 0.66), while the interim overall-survival (OS) difference was not statistically significant. Grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events were more frequent with the triplet regimen (71% versus 32%). EMERALD-1 also reported a PFS benefit for durvalumab plus bevacizumab with TACE, whereas mature OS benefit has not been established. Evidence for TACE-based combinations is more developed than evidence for HAIC-, ablation-, or TARE-based combinations, many of which remain investigational or are supported mainly by nonrandomized studies. Proposed mechanisms include immunogenic cell death, tumor-antigen release, changes in immune-checkpoint signaling, and vascular remodeling. Clinical implementation requires careful patient selection, preservation of hepatic reserve, monitoring for cumulative toxicity, and consideration of quality of life. Ongoing randomized trials, biomarker research, and precision-treatment approaches are expected to clarify which patients benefit from these combinations and how treatment should be sequenced.

item.title: Sample-Handling Bias and Direct ICP-MS of Ultratrace Metals in Semiconductor-Grade Isopropyl Alcohol
item.description:
Abstract
Sample handling can materially affect the reliability of ultratrace elemental analysis even when instrumental precision is adequate. Here, storage-container behavior and a conventional evaporation-to-apparent-dryness/acid-reconstitution procedure were evaluated for metal determination in semiconductor-grade isopropyl alcohol (IPA) by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS). Perfluoroalkoxy alkane (PFA) provided the most stable performance among the tested storage and evaporation vessels, whereas Cr and Sn exhibited reduced recoveries even under room-temperature evaporation conditions. Sequential acid extraction of polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) vessels further revealed incomplete initial recovery and delayed analyte release, consistent with surface-associated retention. To minimize these handling-related effects, a direct matrix-matched standard-addition workflow combining desolvation with oxygen-assisted plasma stabilization was evaluated. Relative to direct analysis without desolvation, the optimized configuration reduced calibration-derived background-equivalent concentrations from 0.25–11.48 to 0.04–5.02 ng kg–1 and increased calibration sensitivity by 4.46–9.21-fold (R2 = 0.9998–1.0000). An existing low-level replicate data set at a 20 ng kg–1 addition level (n = 7), originally acquired for LOD/LOQ evaluation, gave BEC-corrected recoveries of 95.06–104.23% with RSDs of 0.90–5.81%; targeted verification at 100 ng kg–1 (n = 7) gave recoveries of 96.54–102.33% with RSDs ≤3.50%. LODs were 0.77–7.39 ng kg–1. These results show that sample-handling effects should be evaluated alongside instrumental performance when ultratrace impurities are measured in high-purity organic process chemicals. The contribution of this study lies in linking experimentally observed handling-related recovery behavior with a preparation-minimizing analytical workflow rather than in introducing a new desolvation configuration.

item.title: A Fair Exchange? How Hartree–Fock Mixing Governs Ruthenium CO 2 -Photoreduction Models
item.description:
Abstract
The description of CO2 coordination and optical excitation in ruthenium pincer complexes depends on the treatment of exchange and correlation. In this work, we compare seven density functionals for the CNC, NCN, and NNN ligand environments, using MP2 geometries and CC2 excitation energies as references. PBE0 and the double hybrids B2PLYP and PBE0-DH preserve the bent Ru–C-bound adduct across all three complexes and both basis sets considered. PBE0 provides the most favorable compromise between structural accuracy and computational cost. In contrast, M06-2X yields nearly linear CO2 and long Ru–C distances for NCN and NNN even with the larger basis set. Additional calculations show that r2SCAN preserves the bent adduct for both complexes, while the inclusion of empirical dispersion corrections does not alter either outcome. Together with the trends across the other functionals, these results provide strong evidence for a substantial role of exact exchange in destabilizing the bent coordination geometry. The excitation energies, however, cannot be explained by the exact-exchange fraction alone. B2PLYP shows the closest agreement with the principal CC2 absorption bands, despite containing more exact exchange than PBE0, and has larger average perturbative double-excitation corrections than PBE0-DH. Agreement in band positions does not ensure agreement in solar-weighted absorption, for which substantial differences remain, particularly for CNC. Interfragment charge-transfer analysis further identifies which excitations transfer electron density toward CO2, although these descriptors do not determine subsequent photocatalytic activity. Our results indicate that the choice of functional should be assessed separately for coordination geometry, optical absorption, and excited-state charge redistribution.

item.title: Pseudomonas aeruginosa Enhances the Thermal Susceptibility of Staphylococcus aureus in Cocultured Biofilms
item.description:
Abstract
Bacterial biofilms infect medical devices in hundreds of thousands of patients, resist antibiotic treatment, and cost the healthcare industry billions of dollars each year. Generating heat at the biofilm interface is a less-invasive alternative to explantation that has been shown to reduce bacterial populations of common pathogens such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus. Most thermal susceptibility studies to date have investigated single-species biofilms. Although more than 20% of orthopedic infections are polymicrobial, the effect of a second bacterial species on the thermal susceptibility of the other has been largely unknown. To address this, biofilms of Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa were grown as both single-species and polymicrobial biofilms, subjected to a variety of thermal shocks, then selectively enumerated. The long-term elimination of these biofilms was assessed by incubating thermally shocked biofilms under ideal growth conditions for 24 h after heat exposure to test their ability to regrow. Although S. aureus was more thermally resistant than P. aeruginosa in single-species biofilms, its thermal resistance was significantly lowered when grown together with P. aeruginosa. The thermal susceptibility of P. aeruginosa was unaffected by the presence of S. aureus. The reduction of resistance to thermal shock for S. aureus in polymicrobial biofilms did not contribute to complete biofilm elimination, with S. aureus permanently eliminated along with P. aeruginosa only in shocks that were able to eradicate both. Notably, the exposure of polymicrobial biofilms to salt and antibiotics that selectively kill Gram-negative bacteria caused the death of S. aureus in polymicrobial biofilms with P. aeruginosa without affecting single-species S. aureus.

item.title: The Emerging Landscape of Pneumococcal Vaccines: Serotype Replacement, Capsular Polysaccharides, and Next-Generation Approaches for Vaccine Design
item.description:
Abstract
Although pneumococcal conjugate vaccines have markedly reduced the incidence rate of Streptococcus pneumoniae infections, the bacterium still remains a predominant cause of pneumonia, sepsis, meningitis, and otitis media worldwide. Its persistence could be largely attributed to serotype replacement and the emergence of multidrug resistance. S. pneumoniae has more than 100 distinct serotypes, but the available vaccines protect against a limited subset, where uncovered nonvaccine serotypes continue to inflict high mortality and comorbidities especially in children and the elderly. This article has elucidated the role of capsular polysaccharide as the principal determinant of virulence and described its properties including distinct composition, structure, charge, and thickness. It further elaborated how these properties influence the immunogenicity of different serotypes and contribute to their underlying pathophysiology. On the one hand, the negative charge of capsular polysaccharides prevents complement protein-mediated opsonization, and on the other hand, bacteria can dynamically control capsule thickness, balancing immune evasion with colonization. Due to such properties, capsular polysaccharides have been widely utilized for vaccine design. Unlike proteins, capsular polysaccharides are not highly immunogenic and, therefore, coupled with various adjuvants and carrier proteins in different conjugate vaccine formulations. Together, this article reviewed the epidemiology of serotypes, structural composition along with immunogenic features of capsular polysaccharides, and conjugate vaccines. Further, novel vaccine strategies, including expansion of the valency of pneumococcal conjugate vaccines, multiepitope vaccine designs, and protein-based constructs, have been elaborated, which represent pivotal steps toward reducing the infection rate of S. pneumoniae.

item.title: Intelligent Prediction of Tensile Strength of Welds in X70 Pipeline Steel Under Small Sample Gas-phase Hydrogen Filling Conditions Using IWOA-GPR
item.description:
Abstract
The safe operation of hydrogen-enriched natural gas pipelines (HBNG) requires an accurate understanding of the mechanical performance degradation laws of in-service pipeline materials under hydrogen environments. Currently, the experimental data related to the welding materials of in-service X70 pipelines is still relatively limited. The performance degradation behavior under the combined effects of multiple factors such as hydrogen partial pressure, total pressure, and prehydrogening time still lacks accurate characterization and prediction. Therefore, this study conducted slow strain rate tensile (SSRT) tests on in-service X70 pipeline welding materials and used the nitrogen–hydrogen mixed gas, which has been verified for equivalence, instead of the methane-hydrogen mixed gas for gas-phase hydrogen filling, to obtain tensile strength data under different hydrogen partial pressures, total pressures, and prehydrogening time conditions. On this basis, a Gaussian process regression (GPR) prediction model with hydrogen partial pressure, total pressure, and prehydrogening time as input was constructed. To overcome the problem that the empirical setting of GPR hyperparameters is prone to falling into local optimization under small-sample nonlinear data conditions, the improved whale optimization algorithm (IWOA) was introduced to conduct global optimization of the GPR kernel function hyperparameters. The initial population distribution was optimized through Tent mapping, and the global search and local development balance ability of the algorithm was improved by using a Sigmoid nonlinear convergence factor. The results show that the IWOA-GPR model has an RMSE of 3.40 MPa, MAE of 2.93 MPa, and MAPE of 0.41% on the test set; compared with WOA-GPR, Dung Beetle Optimizer-GPR (DBO-GPR), IWOA-KRR, IWOA-XGBoost, and IWOA-SVR, the maximum reduction in MSE and RMSE is 87.5% and 64.6%, respectively, and the accuracy and stability advantages are significant. Further SHAP sensitivity analysis based on the 24 h hydrogen precharging condition indicates that hydrogen partial pressure is the dominant controlling factor (SHAP = 10.11). This study provides an effective data-driven method for predicting the mechanical property degradation of hydrogen-containing pipeline steel under small sample conditions.

item.title: Optimization of Hydrothermal Acid Activation of Coir Fibers: Enhancing Cellulose Yield and Cationic Dye Removal
item.description:
Abstract
The development of sustainable biosorbents from lignocellulosic biomass is often limited by low yield and the energy-intensive fractionation required to enhance specific components and tailor their physicochemical properties for industrial scalability. To address this, an I-optimal response surface methodology (RSM) optimization approach was used to optimize the parameters of the acid-assisted hydrothermal activation process for coir fibers, simultaneously maximizing cellulose yield and methylene blue (MB) removal efficiency. The synergistic effects of acid concentration (0.5–1.0 mol/L), temperature (90–160 °C), activation time (30–150 min), and acid type (HCl, H3PO4) were evaluated. 1.0 mol/L HCl stood out, and the linear model was the best fit for both cases; the acid type influenced MB removal efficiency, while temperature and time negatively impacted the cellulose yield. Optimal conditions (1.0 M HCl, 120 °C, 90 min) achieved a balanced performance with 80.6% cellulose yield and MB removal efficiency (90.7%, 9.07 mg/g). The distinct mesoporous profile framework and the shift of surface charge from 5.8 to 2.1 pHpzc were confirmed by BET surface analysis and the point of zero charge plot. Adsorption of MB onto the surface of the modified coir fiber adsorbents was endothermic chemisorption (ΔH0 = +117.84 kJ/mol) and underwent a spontaneous shift at elevated temperature (45 °C), well fitted by Temkin, Langmuir, pseudo-second-order kinetic (PSO), and intraparticle diffusion (IPD) models for describing the adsorption mechanism. The maximum efficiency (97.82%, 9.78 mg/g) was recorded at the optimum conditions (initial MB concentration = 50 mg/L, dose = 0.5 g/L, pH 11, contact time = 150, temperature 45 °C). Hence, the hydrochar produced in this work has shown promise for scalability.

item.title: The Chemical Bond Overlap Perspective on Halogen Bonds: A Multidescriptor Computational Analysis
item.description:
Abstract
The nature of halogen bonds (XBs) can be described by electrostatic or charge-transfer (CT) models. While orbital overlap has been mentioned as an important component for CT, only visual or indirect measures of orbital overlap have been reported. In this work, we present here a comprehensive multidescriptor computational analysis of X–I···B complexes (where X = F, Cl, Br, I, and B = P(CH3)3, N(CH3)3, C5H5N, NH3, (CH3)2SO, (CH3)2CO, and CH3CN) to investigate the role of constructive orbital interactions in XBs. Employing the OP/TOP framework alongside QTAIM, NBO, and LVM models, we demonstrate how the overlap density describes the CT contribution. The results show that as the B···I interaction strengthens, driven by an n(B) → σ*(I–X) charge transfer, the overlap density (ρOP) and the local stretching force constant (ka) of the I–X bond systematically decrease, while ka increases for the local B···I stretching vibration. Additionally, NBO and OP/TOP indicate that highly electronegative halogens induce the most intense CT. Notably, the OP/TOP framework exhibits distinct sensitivity in differentiating hard and soft Lewis bases. While traditional metrics that capture total bond strength rank the hard NH3 base as an intermediate donor, OP/TOP isolates electron sharing, revealing a lower overlap density for NH3 compared to the softer, more polarizable CH3CN. This study demonstrates that these descriptors are complementary rather than redundant, providing a direct, real-space probe to decouple covalent contributions from electrostatic effects and offering a more comprehensive view of the fundamental interactions governing XBs.

item.title: Engineering Narrow-Bandgap g-C 3 N 4 /AgIn 5 S 8 Heterojunction for Boosted Visible-Light Tetracycline Degradation
item.description:
Abstract
Tetracycline contamination in aquatic environments motivates the development of efficient visible-light-responsive photocatalysts with improved light utilization and interfacial charge-transfer capability. Herein, a narrow-bandgap g-C3N4/AgIn5S8 (NCN-AIS) heterojunction was rationally engineered. Characterization results revealed robust interfacial contact between AgIn5S8 nanoparticles and NCN, with X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and density functional theory (DFT) results suggesting possible In–N-associated interfacial interactions, supporting the successful establishment of the heterojunction interface. Notably, the optimal sample (NCN-AIS-20%) achieved a remarkable tetracycline degradation efficiency of 90.97%, with a reaction rate constant that was 1.4 and 1.8 times higher than those of pristine NCN and AIS, respectively. Besides the enhanced short-wavelength visible-light response and excellent reusability, ultrahigh-performance liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (UHPLC–MS) analysis clearly mapped out the complete stepwise oxidative degradation pathway of tetracycline into CO2 and H2O. Mechanistic insights revealed that the narrow bandgap of the NCN-AIS heterojunction broadened visible light absorption and drastically accelerated photogenerated charge separation and transfer. Radical trapping experiments demonstrated a synergistic effect among h+, •O2–, and •OH, where h+ and •O2– dominated the degradation process. Furthermore, DFT calculations of the difference charge density provided profound theoretical support for the charge transfer mechanism at the atomic level. Consequently, this work not only supplies an efficient photocatalyst for mitigating aqueous antibiotic pollution but also sheds light on the rational design and mechanistic understanding of analogous heterojunction systems.

item.title: Adsorption and Luminescent Properties of a Pyridyl(vinyl)benzoate-Based Zn(II) Coordination Polymer: A Structure–Property Correlation Study
item.description:
Abstract
A new pyridyl(vinyl)benzoate-based zinc(II) coordination polymer, {[Zn(3,4-pvb)2]·DMF·H2O}n (1), was synthesized under solvothermal conditions from {3-[2-(4-pyridyl)vinyl]}benzoic acid (3,4-Hpvb) and Zn(NO3)2·6H2O. The relationship between its structural features, guest adsorption behavior, and photoluminescent properties was investigated. Structural analysis revealed that 1 forms a 3D supramolecular architecture through the noneclipsed stacking of extended corrugated 2D coordination layers, in which Zn(II) centers with distorted pseudotetrahedral geometry are bridged by structurally distinct 3,4-pvb– ligands. This supramolecular arrangement results in limited accessible porosity, with a BET surface area of 9.8 m2 g–1, a pore volume of 0.056 cm3 g–1, and an average pore size of 1.69 nm. Despite its low surface area, compound 1 exhibits adsorption of the polar guest molecules methanol and water, whereas no measurable CO2 uptake was detected under the conditions investigated, highlighting the role of guest–framework interactions in its adsorption behavior. The structural features of 1 are also reflected in its photophysical behavior: its luminescence decay profile displays two lifetime components, consistent with the presence of two structurally distinct 3,4-pvb– ligands in the crystal lattice. Further comparison with the free 3,4-Hpvb proligand revealed that coordination within the framework significantly influences its photochemical behavior. While the emission of 3,4-Hpvb is strongly affected by the solvent and undergoes trans/cis photoisomerization under UV irradiation, this process is strongly suppressed upon coordination and incorporation into the rigid framework of 1. Overall, the results establish a direct relationship between the supramolecular organization of the coordination polymer and its guest adsorption and photophysical behavior.

item.title: Enhanced Coal Spontaneous Combustion Inhibition Using Sodium Silicate-Activated Fly Ash Colloid: Role of Modulus and Concentration
item.description:
Abstract
To develop efficient and low-cost activated fly ash colloids for mine fire prevention and extinguishment, fly ash colloids were modified with sodium silicate (Na2SiO3), and the activation effects of Na2SiO3 were systematically evaluated at six different moduli and seven concentrations. The results show that the reactivity of fly ash was markedly enhanced by Na2SiO3 treatment. At a modulus of 2.2, Al–O bonds in the glassy phase were partially cleaved, promoting the release of soluble Al3+, while the ζ-potential of the system became negative. Meanwhile, abundant silicate ions (SiO32–) and OH– were adsorbed onto particle surfaces, increasing particle electronegativity and facilitating gelation. When the Na2SiO3 concentration was increased to 8%, the fluidity of the fly ash colloid decreased to approximately 65% of its initial value, while interparticle interactions and colloidal cohesion were strengthened, and the gelation time was markedly shortened. Under the optimized conditions of a modulus of 2.2 and a concentration of 8%, the CO generation rate of coal samples coated with the Na2SiO3-activated fly ash colloid was reduced by 84.72% compared with raw coal, and the inhibition rate reached 77.47%. These findings demonstrate that fly ash colloids can be effectively activated by Na2SiO3, enabling enhanced oxygen isolation, reduced reactivity of active functional groups, and effective prevention of coal spontaneous combustion.

item.title: Symmetry and Anion Composition Effects on HDABCO-based Ferroelectric Ionic Plastic Crystals
item.description:
Abstract
Ferroelectric ionic plastic crystals represent an exciting opportunity for nontoxic electrical energy storage materials. While plastic crystals exhibit a high-temperature mesophase in which the molecular components have rotational freedom, our understanding and control of molecular rotation are limited. Here, we have systematically changed the anion in the ferroelectric ionic plastic crystal [HDABCO]ClO4, with smaller and larger anionic species, BF4– and ReO4–, respectively. Using machine-learned force fields (MLFFs) derived from density functional theory (DFT), we have performed molecular dynamics (MD) simulations on the compounds, in order to investigate anion rotation and proton disorder on the atomistic scale. The rotation of the anions goes through three distinct phases; oscillation around minima positions, ligand reorientation motion, and full rotation in the high-temperature phase, where the rotational speed is correlated with anion size and crystal packing fraction. The proton transfer is calculated to reach THz frequency range at room temperature due to the low energy barrier for proton hopping, and both [HDABCO]ClO4 and [HDABCO]BF4 show significant positional disorder of the proton below the phase transition temperature. Anion substitution can enable tuning of the rotational and proton positional order of HDABCO-based ionic plastic crystals.

item.title: Laser-Reduced Graphene Oxide Electrodes as a Self-Stabilizing Scaffold for Neat Ionic Liquids in Humidity Sensing
item.description:
Abstract
Ionic liquids (ILs) are attractive sensing materials for humidity detection because of their hydrophilicity and their highly tunable physicochemical properties. However, most reported IL-based humidity sensors require an additional immobilization matrix, such as a polymer, nanoparticle composite, or poly(ionic liquid), to stabilize the liquid phase on solid-state electrodes, thereby increasing fabrication complexity. Here, we report capacitive humidity sensors based on neat 1-hexyl-1-methyl-2-(3-pyridinyl)pyrrolidinium methanesulfonate ([HexNic][MeSO3]) directly immobilized within porous laser-reduced graphene oxide (LRGO) interdigitated electrodes. Graphene oxide (GO) was laser-reduced using a CO2 laser to produce a highly porous LRGO structure containing 92 atom % C and 8 atom % O. The IL was subsequently drop-cast onto the electrodes and retained within the porous LRGO network without the need for an additional immobilization matrix. At the optimal IL loading, the resulting sensors exhibited a sensitivity of 1650 pF/% RH, with response and recovery times of 180 and 33 s, respectively. The devices also showed very low hysteresis, with a maximum value of 1.01% RH and stable capacitive performance over 30 days. The humidity-sensing mechanism was elucidated by using complex impedance spectroscopy and attenuated total reflectance-Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR-ATR). As a proof of concept, the sensor was further applied to respiratory monitoring and successfully distinguished between slow- and fast-breathing patterns. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of a neat IL directly immobilized within a porous graphene-based electrode for capacitive humidity sensing without an additional polymeric or composite matrix. The approach provides a simple and scalable route to high-performance IL-based humidity sensors.

item.title: Predicting Physiological-Level Glucose In Vitro with Terahertz ATR Spectroscopy: A Study of Robust Calibration
item.description:
Abstract
Noninvasive glucose sensing has been the focus of extensive optical research, yet terahertz (THz) spectroscopy remains comparatively underexplored for reliable glucose quantification at physiological concentrations. This is partly because aqueous THz measurements are strongly affected by experimental variability, which can obscure the weak glucose-induced spectral response. In this study, we investigate whether standard THz time-domain spectroscopy (TDS) in an attenuated total reflection (ATR) geometry can provide reliable, physically interpretable, and generalizable in vitro glucose quantification in liquid samples at physiological concentrations. Glucose solutions at physiological concentrations were measured in phosphate-buffered saline, deionized water, and artificial interstitial fluid to evaluate the reproducibility of the glucose-induced spectral response across optically distinct sample matrices. By combining simultaneous amplitude and phase detection with a randomized experimental protocol, differential THz-ATR spectra were used to isolate glucose-induced spectral contrast from systematic experimental effects. The differential spectra showed a reproducible glucose-dependent response across matrices, with amplitude and phase trends that followed the expected optical response of aqueous glucose solutions. Partial least-squares regression was used to assess quantitative glucose prediction and calibration generalizability. The results demonstrate that glucose-induced spectral contrast can be reproducibly retrieved across liquid matrices and used for prediction at physiological concentrations. Both pooled-matrix regression and cross-matrix calibration transfer further indicate that the calibration models can generalize across matrix conditions, with replicate repeatability remaining a key factor governing performance. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of robust and physically interpretable in vitro glucose quantification in liquids at physiological concentrations using standard THz-TDS. These results provide a critical first step toward clarifying the role of THz spectroscopy in glucose sensing, from liquid-phase model systems to future transdermal applications.

item.title: Numerical Simulation Study on Fracture Height Growth in Shale Reservoirs with Shell Interbeds
item.description:
Abstract
Shell interbeds are vertically developed in the shale reservoirs of Da’anzhai Member of Block X. Vertical changes in the in-situ stress and mechanical properties of the reservoir induced by shell limestone interbeds can suppress the fracture height growth, thereby affecting the fracturing effect of shale reservoirs. To elucidate the propagation mechanisms of fractures in shell-interbedded shale reservoirs, based on whole-rock mineral analysis and rock mechanics experimental results, the finite element simulation is employed to investigate the influence of interbed stress difference, interbed thickness, injection distance, displacement rate, and fluid viscosity on the fracture height growth in such reservoirs. Additionally, the fracture propagation morphologies under various distribution patterns of multiple shell interbeds are compared and analyzed. The results indicate that the greater the interbed stress difference, the thicker the interbed, and the farther the injection distance, the more difficult it is for fractures to penetrate through the layers. An increase in the displacement rate and viscosity is conducive to the penetration of fractures through the interbeds. When multiple shell interbeds are hosted in shale, the increase in fracture height is significantly affected by the distribution of the shell interbeds. The results can offer theoretical guidance for the design of fracturing schemes for shell-interbedded shale reservoirs.

item.title: Study on the Uniaxial Compressive Mechanical Properties and Instability Mechanism of Fractured Coal–Rock Composite Bodies
item.description:
Abstract
In coal–rock systems, the weak interlayer zones between coal and rock strata are primary regions for fracture distribution, and the presence of fractures within the coal significantly influences the mechanical properties and engineering stability of coal–rock assemblages. Therefore, investigating the mechanical behavior and failure characteristics of coal–rock assemblages containing fractured coal is of great significance for controlling the stability of deep coal–rock engineering projects and preventing dynamic disasters. To investigate the impact of fractured coal on the mechanical characteristics of coal–rock systems, uniaxial compression experiments were conducted on coal–rock composite bodies with different fracture angles. The results indicate that as the fracture inclination angle increased from 0° to 90°, the average peak strength of the composites rose from 6.41 to 13.09 MPa; however, these values remained significantly lower than that of the intact composite (22.56 MPa), representing a reduction of 41.71% to 71.59%. During the uniaxial compression process, the internal energy of the samples is converted into the expansion of macroscopic cracks, and the failure modes are primarily tensile failure and shear failure. The total energy and dissipated energy of the composite specimens increase with the fracture angle, with the total elastic strain energy being greater than the dissipated energy at the point of failure. By analyzing the energy accumulation and transfer processes of the coal and rock during loading, the accumulation and distribution patterns of elastic strain energy under loading were revealed. An energy transfer model for fissured coal–rock composites was established, and the energy transfer and fissure evolution mechanisms during the instability and failure process of the composite were analyzed. The results provide valuable references for understanding the mechanical properties of deep coal–rock systems and the mechanisms of dynamic disasters.

item.title: Attenuated Total Reflection Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy and Chemometrics for the Forensic Investigation of Intentional Rodenticide Poisoning in Ground and Liquid Coffee
item.description:
Abstract
Advances in forensic science and analytical technologies have significantly improved the collection, preservation, and interpretation of material evidence. Food and beverage matrices can serve as valuable forensic evidence when biological samples are absent or degraded. Among these matrices, coffee is particularly relevant to investigations of intentional poisoning because its sensory characteristics can mask toxic substances. Pesticides marketed as rodenticides, including carbamate and organophosphate compounds, together with the anticoagulant rodenticide brodifacoum, are of forensic interest because of their toxicity, widespread use, and occurrence in poisoning cases. Traditional chromatographic techniques, while robust and sensitive, are costly and labor-intensive, and many forensic laboratories face limited access to such equipment. Attenuated Total Reflection Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (ATR-FTIR) combined with chemometric tools such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Soft Independent Modeling of Class Analogy (SIMCA) offers a rapid, nondestructive, and cost-effective alternative for screening rodenticide-related contamination in complex matrices. This study evaluated the potential of ATR-FTIR coupled with chemometric analysis for detecting rodenticide-related contamination in coffee and its applicability to forensic investigations of intentional poisoning. Commercial brodifacoum-based rodenticides and rodenticide formulations of unknown composition were investigated as representative toxic agents. A preliminary evaluation of ground coffee contaminated with one unknown formulation at 5.0 and 10.0% (w/w) was conducted to define the experimental conditions. The 5.0% level was selected for subsequent analyses because it was the lower of the two evaluated levels and already provided multivariate differentiation from uncontaminated samples. A total of 85 ground-coffee observations and 84 liquid-coffee observations were initially evaluated. Following Hotelling’s T2/Q-SPE assessment and inspection of the original spectral profiles, the refined data sets were used for exploratory and supervised multivariate analyses. Three SIMCA-based decision rules, data-driven SIMCA (DD-SIMCA), alternative SIMCA (Alt-SIMCA), and a Hotelling’s T2-only rule, were evaluated using the corrected spectral range for ground coffee or the full spectral range for liquid coffee, as well as the fingerprint region from 1800 to 900 cm–1, with external-validation sets comprising 26 to 28 samples depending on the matrix and spectral region. For ground coffee, both DD-SIMCA and Alt-SIMCA achieved 100% external-validation accuracy and 100% sensitivity for all classes in both spectral regions, with specificities of at least 75.00% and 80.00%, respectively. For liquid coffee, the best performance was obtained with Alt-SIMCA using the full spectral range, which achieved 100% external-validation accuracy, 100% sensitivity for all classes, and class specificities ranging from 89.47 to 100%. Within the tested formulations, coffee brands, and contamination level, these findings indicate the potential of ATR-FTIR combined with chemometrics as a rapid screening tool for the forensic analysis of coffee samples suspected of contamination with toxic agents.

item.title: Synchronized Twisting, Helical Conformation, and Reduced Symmetry in Alcalde’s Zwitterions: Early Saturation of First Hyperpolarizability before Peierls Distortion
item.description:
Abstract
This work reports structure–property correlations for a series of pyridinium imidazolate-based zwitterions. With initial HF/6–31G computations (based on an earlier report: excellent agreement between the experiment and computation), hyperpolarizabilities (β) were found to be abnormally large (β0 ≈ 0.15 million × 10–30 esu and |μβ| ≈ 12 million × 10-48 esu). However, when reinvestigated with the HF, B3LYP, and CAM-B3LYP methodologies (combined with the 6-31G(d,p) basis set), drastic reductions in hyperpolarizabilities were observed. In general, saturations of hyperpolarizabilities were observed with two or three bridging benzene rings (CAM-B3LYP: β0 ≈ 4054.0 × 10–30 esu and |μβ| ≈ 0.2 million × 10–48 esu; although these are among the largest values reported in the literature, they need further experimental verification). Observations of such large hyperpolarizabilities and early saturations were found to occur before the Peierls distortion point. Also, many molecules showed absorptions in near- to far-IR regions, thus capable of providing solutions to the transparency trade-off problem existing in nonlinear optics. Nevertheless, we propose how the gyratory nature of the inter-ring junctions can be synchronized in a helical fashion in a tunable structural topography to control the intramolecular interactions and to induce the optimal hyperpolarizabilities (and saturation limit) and transparency trade-off problem of nonlinear optics.

item.title: Penijavanicins A and B, Complex Polycyclic Polyketides Featuring a cis -Fused Dihydroisocoumarin-Tetrahydropyran Core with Anti-Neuroinflammatory Activity
item.description:
Abstract
Chemical investigation of the soil-derived fungus Penicillium sp. 16F038 using the One Strain Many Compounds (OSMAC) strategy led to the discovery of penijavanicins A and B (1 and 2), two structurally novel aromatic polyketides. Comprehensive spectroscopic analyses, including 1,1-ADEQUATE NMR and HRESIMS, established their planar structures as an unprecedented 6/6/6/6/6 pentacyclic framework incorporating a cis-fused dihydroisocoumarin-tetrahydropyran architecture. The challenging stereochemical assignments, posed by the densely functionalized and conformationally constrained core, were successfully resolved through O-methylation derivatization, quantitative ROESY analysis, and TDDFT-ECD calculations. Biological evaluations revealed that compound 2 displayed significant antineuroinflammatory activity in LPS-stimulated BV-2 microglial cells by markedly suppressing nitric oxide (NO), TNF-α and IL-6 production without appreciable cytotoxicity. Furthermore, network pharmacology, molecular docking, and Western blot analyses suggested that 2 exerts its anti-inflammatory effects by inhibiting the ERK/NF-κB signaling pathway.

item.title: Correction to “Mechanistic Insights into Rare Earth Element Dissolution from Sart (Manisa) Black Sand via Alkali Roasting–Acid Leaching”
item.description: Bibliographic inaccuracies were identified in refs 1−8. As such, we are making corrections to the details for these articles to preserve the accuracy of the academic record. These corrections are limited to bibliographic information associated with the affected references and do not affect the experimental data, results, scientific interpretation, discussion, or conclusions of the published article. We apologize for the oversight and any unintentional inconvenience caused.

item.title: Study on the Wetting Properties of Coal Dust Based on Sedimentation Behavior and Selection of Optimal Surfactants
item.description:
Abstract
Spray dust suppression in coal mines relies on the wetting of coal particles by the spray liquid. Most screening tests, however, assess only the first droplet–coal contact, although in practice coal dust undergoes repeated wetting, drying, and rewetting. A sedimentation-based protocol then treats initial wetting and the rewetting of dried, modified coal dust in deionized water as two independent dimensions. Twelve monomeric surfactants of four classes were screened at six concentrations (0.02–0.20 wt %), and the best were blended in equal volumes. Coal dust of two size fractions (d ≤ 0.150 and 0.075 mm) from the Chengzihe Coal Mine was tested, with the settling rate as a dynamic wetting proxy. Surfactant ranking differed between the stages and reversed with particle size, so a single contact measurement cannot predict field performance. A reproducible inflection at 0.04–0.06 wt % defined a practical concentration range. For coarse dust, monomers generally outperformed the blends (OP-10 and FPA-T strongest in initial wetting); for fine dust, the blends were superior, and FPA-T+AOS was the only system effective in both stages, making it the most suitable additive for the fine fraction. Contact angle, FTIR, and zeta potential explained this static–dynamic mismatch, providing a particle-size-dependent basis for additive selection.

item.title: In-Process Application of Cellulose Nanofibrils Suited for Molded Fiber Substrates: Spreading during Pulsed Underwater Jet Deposition
item.description:
Abstract
Molded fiber products require PFAS-free technologies that provide oil and grease resistance. Cellulose nanofibrils (CNFs) are renewable barrier materials, but conventional coating methods are generally limited to flat substrates and require separate coating and drying operations, restricting their application to three-dimensional molded fiber products. In-process CNF application has the potential to reduce the need for these additional operations, but the spreading behavior of pulsed underwater CNF deposition during dewatering has not been systematically examined. This study investigated the effects of CNF solids content, jet velocity, nozzle diameter, and nozzle-to-substrate distance on pulsed underwater CNF deposition onto submerged porous paperboard. Laboratory experiments, complemented by finite-element simulations using a Papanastasiou-regularized Bingham model, showed that the 0.3 and 0.5 wt % CNF suspensions produced the greatest area coverage, whereas the 0.8 wt % suspension exhibited reduced coverage and a pronounced center-heavy coat-weight distribution. Nozzle diameter also influenced area coverage, with its effect dependent on jet velocity, while nozzle-to-substrate distance had comparatively little influence over the range investigated. The simulations generally captured the observed spreading behavior, although the level of agreement between predicted and experimental coverage varied with CNF solids content and operating conditions. Dimensionless analysis using the Reynolds number, incorporating concentration-dependent apparent viscosity, showed a strong correlation with normalized area coverage (R2 = 0.91). CNF-covered regions achieved a Kit value of 12, demonstrating effective grease resistance within the covered areas. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of controlled pulsed underwater CNF deposition during dewatering and provide a basis for further evaluation of in-process CNF surface functionalization for molded fiber products.

item.title: A Cardanol-Derived Fluorescent Marker Based on aza-BODIPY for Petroleum Fuel Tagging
item.description:
Abstract
A new petroleum marker (BDPC) was successfully synthesized from cardanol, a renewable feedstock obtained from cashew nut shell liquid, an abundant byproduct of the cashew processing industry. The incorporation of lipophilic cardanol chains enhanced the marker’s compatibility with nonpolar petroleum fuels, facilitating its incorporation into fuel matrices. BDPC exhibited near-infrared fluorescence maxima at 700 nm in hexane and 710 nm in diesel and E10 gasoline, enabling selective detection with minimal interference from fuel matrices. At an optimal concentration (3 ppm), the marker caused no visible change in the fuels while remaining readily detectable by ultraviolet–visible and fluorescence spectroscopy. Fluorescence measurements showed a linear response within the low-ppm range, supporting sensitive quantitative analysis. Physicochemical evaluations by the American Society for Testing and Materials indicated that incorporating BDPC did not substantially alter fuel properties, including volatility, viscosity, density, sulfur content, and cetane index. In addition, the fluorescence intensity of BDPC remained stable in diesel and E10 gasoline for at least 90 days. These findings reveal the promising potential of BDPC as a sustainable, durable, and nondisruptive marker for practical applications in petroleum authentication and traceability.

item.title: Catalyst-Mediated Nucleation Control in Chemical Vapor Transport Growth of Black Phosphorus: A Comprehensive Raman Study
item.description:
Abstract
Black phosphorus (BP) synthesized via Sn–I-assisted chemical vapor transport (CVT) is susceptible to structural inhomogeneity and oxidation-related defects that limit its crystalline quality. We systematically investigate the influence of transition metal additives (Fe, Co, Cu, and Ag) on BP structural properties during growth in the temperature range 600–700 °C. Raman spectroscopy was employed to evaluate vibrational mode positions, line widths, and disorder-activated features across multiple growth conditions. Among all investigated metals, Fe-assisted growth at 650 °C yielded the narrowest full width at half-maximum (FWHM) for the A1g, B2g, and A2g phonon modes, accompanied by the suppression of oxide vibrational features near 900 cm–1 and the absence of low-wavenumber disorder-induced modes. In contrast, Cu-, Co-, and Ag-assisted growth exhibits broader line widths, increased spectral variability, and additional defect-related signatures, particularly at 600 and 700 °C. These results establish a comparative framework for metal-mediated CVT synthesis and identify Fe as an effective additive for improving BP structure and lattice coherence.

item.title: Energy–Dose Optimization and Substrate Effects in Ion-Induced Graphene Nanopore Creation
item.description:
Abstract
Ion irradiation of graphene involves a trade-off among controlled nanopore formation, collateral defect generation, and retained mechanical integrity. Here, molecular dynamics simulations are used to establish a first-order quantitative guideline linking ion energy, ion dose, and target pore geometry for argon-ion-induced nanopore formation in free-standing graphene. By mapping this coupled dependence, we identify the threshold conditions for complete pore opening and the energetically favorable pathways toward prescribed pore sizes. Substrate thickness and substrate type are found to alter sputtering through two competing mechanisms: at low and intermediate energies, the substrate suppresses net damage by limiting atom escape and promoting rapid recombination, whereas at higher energies, recoil and backscattering enhance carbon displacement. We further show that the mechanical strength of nanoporous graphene is strongly reduced when irradiation-induced defects form near the pore edge, because of amplified local stress concentration and earlier crack initiation. These results provide a unified description of pore opening thresholds, energy optimization, substrate-mediated damage evolution, and defect-controlled mechanical weakening in ion-irradiated graphene.

item.title: 2D Materials as SERS Substrates for the Detection of DNA and its Constituents
item.description:
Abstract
Surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) has emerged as a powerful ultrasensitive and label-free analytical technique for the detection of nucleic acids, including DNA and its constituents. Although conventional noble-metal-based substrates such as gold and silver provide strong electromagnetic enhancement, their practical implementation is often limited by chemical instability, reproducibility issues, and biocompatibility concerns. In recent years, two-dimensional (2D) materials have attracted growing interest as alternative or hybrid SERS platforms due to their atomically thin architectures, high surface-to-volume ratios, tunable electronic properties, and their ability to facilitate charge-transfer-driven chemical enhancement. This review highlights recent advances in the application of representative 2D materials, including graphene, molybdenum disulfide (MoS2), and black phosphorene (BP), for SERS-based detection of DNA and its constituents. Unlike previous reviews that primarily focus on plasmonic SERS substrates or provide a broad overview of 2D materials, this review presents a dedicated comparative analysis of graphene, MoS2, and BP for DNA-related SERS applications. Particular emphasis is placed on correlating enhancement mechanisms, sensing performance, and reported limits of detection (LODs) to identify the strengths, limitations, and future opportunities of each material platform. Their enhancement mechanisms, sensing performance, stability, and biocompatibility are comparatively analyzed. Graphene demonstrates excellent chemical stability and fluorescence quenching capability, while MoS2 offers versatile surface chemistry and efficient integration with plasmonic nanostructures. Black phosphorene has shown particularly strong chemical enhancement effects, attributed to favorable interfacial charge-transfer interactions with nucleic acid molecules. Finally, current challenges and future perspectives are discussed to guide the rational design of robust and high-performance SERS substrates for applications in molecular diagnostics, DNA sequencing, and biomedical analysis.

item.title: How Far Do Kamlet–Taft Parameters and pH Predict Delignification by Deep Eutectic Solvents?
item.description:
Abstract
Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) are tunable, low-toxicity media for lignocellulose fractionation, but their selection for delignification still relies on empirical screening. Kamlet–Taft (KT) solvatochromic parameters (hydrogen-bond acidity α, basicity β, and dipolarity/polarizability π*) and pH are the descriptors most often correlated with lignin solubility, yet how far they predict delignification of whole biomass has not been tested critically. Here we report measured KT parameters and apparent pH (pHapp) for 56 DES formulations spanning carboxylic-acid, polyol, metal-salt, amide, alkanolamine, and amino-acid families, together with the softwood lignin removal obtained after a sequential enzymatic–DES fractionation. Four descriptor-to-performance models were compared under identical leave-one-out, repeated k-fold, and grouped (leave-one-cluster-out and leave-one-family-out) cross-validation: a linear correlation, a 15-term second-order polynomial, a random forest (RF), and a Gaussian-process (GP) regressor with automatic relevance determination. All models fit the training set (in-sample R2 up to 0.89 for the RF) but generalize weakly: leave-one-out R2 is 0.10–0.13 for the GP and the RF, the polynomial is overparameterized and generalizes worse than the training mean, and no model predicts a chemical family that is absent from training better than the training mean. Gaussian-process relevance and ablation and random-forest permutation importance rank pHapp as the most informative descriptor, followed by α, whereas β and π* carry little consistent information, and the pKa of the hydrogen-bond donor carries the same information as pHapp; these results point to solvent acid strength, rather than hydrogen-bond donation alone, as the property most closely associated with lignin removal from enzymatically pretreated softwood. The GP provides calibrated predictive uncertainty: 96% of leave-one-out predictions and all four prospectively synthesized blind-test DESs fall within its 95% credible intervals. The results delimit what solvatochromic descriptors can and cannot predict for whole-biomass delignification and provide an uncertainty-aware screening tool and an open data set for DES design.

item.title: Pyrolysis-Side Study for a Proposed Integrated Heavy-Oil Pyrolysis and Coke-Gasification Process: Effects of Temperature and Initial Syngas Pressure
item.description:
Abstract
A pyrolysis-side study was conducted to clarify how thermal severity and initial syngas pressure influence product redistribution and coke structure during heavy-oil conversion, providing experimental guidance for a proposed integrated pyrolysis–coke-gasification concept without claiming validation of the complete recycle process. Canadian oil-sands bitumen was pyrolyzed at 400–500 °C and initial syngas pressures of 0.5–5 MPa with a fixed CO/H2 volume ratio of 2:3. Pyrolysis temperature had the strongest effect on product distribution. As the temperature increased from 400 to 500 °C, the oil yield decreased from 46.67 to 22.13 wt %, while gas and coke yields increased. Approximately complete conversion was reached at 450 °C, whereas further heating mainly promoted secondary cracking and condensation. At 450 °C, increasing the initial syngas pressure from 0.5 to 5 MPa increased the oil yield from 29.86 to 35.53 wt % and reduced gas and coke yields by 3.62 and 2.05 wt %, respectively. The increase in liquid yield was mainly associated with an 11.72 wt % increase in VGO, accompanied by lower gasoline and diesel yields, indicating that higher pressure favored the retention of heavier liquid intermediates. Coke produced at higher temperatures was more condensed, more ordered, and less reactive, whereas higher syngas pressure resulted in a more disordered and functionalized carbon structure with higher oxidation reactivity. An exploratory composite structure–reactivity descriptor showed a strong within-data set association with the air-oxidation index (R2 = 0.9791; Q2LOO = 0.9498); however, the relationship is based on only eight unique operating conditions and requires external validation before predictive generalization. Considering conversion, product distribution, pressure severity, and coke reactivity, 450 °C and 1 MPa were retained as a reasonable bench-scale reference among the tested conditions, rather than as a temperature–pressure optimum.

item.title: Electrochemical Quantification of Salivary Amyloid-β1–42 Using Disposable Gold Screen-Printed Electrodes: Analytical Validation and Comparison with ELISA
item.description:
Abstract
Sensitive quantification of low-abundance biomarkers in noninvasive biofluids is critical for advancing Alzheimer’s disease (AD) diagnostics. In this study, we developed an electrochemical immunosensor for the detection of amyloid β 1–42 (Aβ1–42) in human saliva using disposable gold screen-printed electrodes (AuSPEs). The sensing interface was fabricated through covalent antibody immobilization on a cysteamine-modified gold surface to enable selective electrochemical recognition of Aβ1–42. Under optimized conditions, the immunosensor exhibited a linear response over the concentration range of 10–40 pg/mL with a limit of detection of 5.39 pg/mL and good selectivity toward structurally related peptides. To reduce matrix-associated signal variability during saliva analysis, a simple PBS dilution protocol was applied, resulting in reduced intersubject signal variability compared with untreated saliva samples (SD ≤ 3.05 μA) and a strong correlation with PBS measurements (R2 = 0.9962). The developed platform demonstrated the feasibility of electrochemical detection of low-abundance Aβ1–42 in diluted human saliva using disposable electrodes. Furthermore, pilot application using 25 human saliva specimens demonstrated strong linear concordance with a commercial ELISA benchmark (R2 = 0.9817), supporting the analytical reliability and preliminary feasibility of this noninvasive platform for salivary Aβ1–42 measurement.

item.title: Enhancing Removal of PFAS and Pharmaceuticals from Municipal Wastewater via GAC Pretreatment and StyDex Polishing
item.description:
Abstract
A dual-sorbent system consisting of a granular activated carbon (GAC) pretreatment followed by polishing with styrene-functionalized β-cyclodextrin (StyDex) beads was evaluated for removal of four per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS: PFOA, PFHxA, PFBA and PFHxS) and two pharmaceuticals, bezafibrate (BEZ) and diclofenac (DCF), from municipal wastewater. Building on previous pilot evaluations of StyDex as a stand-alone sorbent, this study evaluates its integration into a treatment train with GAC pretreatment, examining GAC replacement frequency and selection of polishing sorbent to more effectively remove mixtures of PFAS and other trace organic contaminants from municipal wastewater. Upstream GAC pretreatment was used to nonselectively remove target compounds, dissolved organic carbon (DOC), and other competing background wastewater constituents to enhance downstream polishing performance. System performance was evaluated by comparing individual removal of target compounds by GAC-StyDex and GAC-ion-exchange resin (IXR) treatment trains and assessing the impact of periodic GAC replacement on polishing performance. Combining GAC pretreatment with StyDex polishing demonstrated the highest total removal of PFOA, PFHxS, and DCF over the duration of the pilot, and improved removal of the weaker sorbing compounds, PFHxA, BEZ, and PFBA. However, PFBA was not effectively controlled over the full pilot duration and exhibited substantially lower cumulative removal (55%–62%) in the GAC-StyDex and GAC-IXR trains, compared to the other five target compounds, which all had >93% removal. Extending the GAC replacement interval from 2,500 to 5,000 BV increased sorption capacity by 59.9% (0.177 to 0.283 μmol g–1), allowing greater GAC bed utilization prior to replacement while also maintaining low effluent concentrations after polishing. Compared with GAC-IXR, GAC-StyDex had 87.4% greater sorption capacity (0.283 vs 0.151 μmol g–1) on a mass-normalized basis and similar performance on a sorbent-volume basis, demonstrating StyDex as a high-capacity alternative sorbent for downstream polishing. These findings demonstrate the potential for integrating GAC pretreatment with downstream polishing to improve contaminant removal, maintain low effluent concentrations, enhance sorbent utilization, and inform the design of scalable wastewater treatment systems.

item.title: Thermodynamics of Exchange Reactions of Heterometallic Mg and Ca Carbonate Nanoclusters
item.description:
Abstract
Density functional theory (DFT) and correlated molecular orbital theory (CCSD(T)) methods were used to investigate aqueous-phase heterometallic substitution in (MgCO3)n and (CaCO3)n nanoclusters containing two to four MCO3, yielding (M′CO3)(MCO3)(n−1) clusters (n = 2−4), where M = Mg or Ca and M′ = Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Zn, Cd, or Hg. Solvation free energies were predicted using the CPCM model, a self-consistent reaction field (SCRF) method. The Mg- and Ca-based mixed-metal clusters generally prefer structures similar to (MgCO3)n and (CaCO3)n for n = 2−4, with most metal centers having a metal−O coordination number (CN) of 4. Aqueous binding free energies for the isodesmic exchange of M′CO3 units into (MCO3)n were calculated. The binding free energies of the larger alkaline-earth M′CO3 are favorable in the Mg-based and unfavorable in the Ca-based nanoclusters, whereas exchange of most 3d and Group 12 M′CO3 units is favorable, driven mainly by the strong solvation of the MgCO3 and CaCO3 products. The predicted substitution free energies of the hydrated Group 2 and 3d transition and Group 12 metal dications [M(H2O)m]2+ were predicted to correspond with H2O release upon substitution, solvation effects, and ionic radius.

item.title: Green Electrochemical Synthesis of Antimicrobial Polyaldehyde Starch
item.description:
Abstract
Conventional aldehyde-based biocides raise environmental and safety concerns due to their toxicity and persistence in inhibiting microbiologically influenced corrosion (MIC) in numerous industrial applications. The present study introduces a rapid and sustainable method for synthesizing polyaldehyde starch through electrochemistry (PAS-EC) using soluble starch as feedstock in aqueous salt media with iridium–ruthenium electrodes. This approach has the potential to replace toxic oxidants with a safer alternative, while significantly reducing reaction time and enhancing overall process safety. By minimizing hazardous reagents and streamlining operational steps, it can also contribute to improved sustainability. Taken together, these features make electrochemical methods a promising pathway for application in industrial bioprocesses. Under optimized electrochemical conditions (15 mA cm–2, 15% NaCl, and 1 h), PAS-EC was obtained with 65% yield and a degree of oxidation exceeding 63%, surpassing the conventional periodate-oxidized dialdehyde starch (DAS-PO) with 50% yield and a 48% degree of oxidation. FTIR and NMR characterization confirmed the successful formation of aldehydic groups, while thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) revealed a decrease in thermal stability due to the modification in the structure of pure starch. Biocidal efficacy was assessed against six hydrocarbon-degrading bacterial strains that are extremely relevant to MIC and bioremediation under oil and gas field conditions. PAS-EC displayed promising and broad-spectrum antibacterial activity, with a maximum of 60% inhibition efficiency at 1000 ppm in comparison to glutaraldehyde. Overall, both PAS-EC and DAS-PO demonstrated promising biocidal performance, underscoring their potential as safer and more sustainable alternatives.

item.title: Tau Disaggregation by a CNS-Permeable Small Molecule Reduces Fibril and Oligomer Burden and Preserves Proteostasis and Behavior
item.description:
Abstract
Pathological aggregates of the microtubule-associated protein, tau, drive neuronal dysfunction in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and related tauopathies. Yet, strategies to slow or eliminate progressive accumulation of misfolded tau protein in the brain remain underdeveloped relative to upstream therapeutic approaches, such as amyloid-beta (Aβ) immunotherapy. Here, we explore a coumarin-based series of brain-permeable small molecules that disaggregate tau. Structure–activity relationships (SAR) identified nitrile-containing analogs as potential leads from the series and suggest a stacking-driven disassembly mechanism. Small molecules from this series disaggregated tau from AD brain-derived matter, reducing aggregate burden measured in vitro across both fibrillar and oligomeric tau species, two principal pathological aggregate species implicated in disease. Mechanistic studies demonstrate that disaggregation does not generate soluble oligomeric intermediates, addressing a central question in the field. Inhibitor treatment reduces prion-like seeding, a disease-related mechanism by which tau aggregation pathology spreads in the brain. The lead candidate from this series is well tolerated in vivo, which enabled efficacy testing in a tauopathy mouse model. Treatment reduced tau pathology while preserving behavioral function, proteasome capacity, and synaptic integrity. These findings establish small-molecule tau disaggregation as a viable therapeutic strategy and provide a mechanistic framework for the design of aggregate-directed therapeutics in neurodegeneration.

item.title: Oxidation of Water and Hydroxide by Graphite Fluoride
item.description:
Abstract
Graphite fluoride is defluorinated by water at high and neutral pH under subcritical conditions. The solid carbon product is unusual in that it is largely graphitic but also contains nanoscale linear hydrocarbon segments. The high pH system is strongly oxidizing, and some carbon is removed as CO32–. Carbon–carbon bonds in partially defluorinated materials are destabilized, and cyclic fluorocarbons are released on heating to as low as 200 °C. The relationship to Li-(CF)x battery technology is discussed.

item.title: Aqueous • OH Kinetics of Gluconic, Glucuronic, and Galacturonic Acids and Lifetimes in Cloudwater
item.description:
Abstract
Reactions of hydroxyl radicals (•OH) with organic compounds strongly influence the formation and evolution of organic aerosols, cloudwater chemistry, and the oxidative capacity of water in natural and engineered environments. In this work, bimolecular reaction rate constants (kOH, M–1 s–1) for aqueous •OH reaction with the environmentally widespread sugar acids (SAs): gluconic, glucuronic, and galacturonic acids in the temperature range between 278 and 318 K were measured. The measurements were performed with the laser flash photolysis–long-path absorption technique for undissociated (AH) and dissociated (A¯) forms of SAs. At 298 K, the measured kOH values ranged from 1.0 to 1.3 × 109 M–1 s–1, with higher reactivity observed for carboxylates. The values of activation parameters were characteristic of the •OH reaction with saturated water-soluble organic compounds (WSOCs) and revealed an enthalpy (ΔH‡)–entropy (ΔS‡) compensation for AH and A¯ forms of SAs. A¯ forms of SAs exhibited lower activation energies, ΔH‡, and more negative ΔS‡ values, uncharacteristic of other C4–C6 saturated acids. Such behavior was consistent with long-range effects of acid dissociation, potentially involving electronic, conformational, and H-bonding effects. kOH values predicted for SAs with two structure–activity relationships (SARs) were overestimated up to 3.5 times, due to the lack of parametrization for the unique electronic effects of adjacent −OH moieties. The intramolecular selectivity of •OH reaction with SAs was analyzed with SARs and density functional theory (DFT). Both methods indicated a preferential H atom abstraction by •OH from the C–H bonds further away from the acidic moiety. DFT results showed that −COOH dissociation affects the energy barriers for H atom abstraction through the (poly)hydroxylated carbon chain, consistent with a long-range electronic effect. Obtained kinetic data revealed that the •OH reaction with SAs can contribute to their removal in remote, marine, and some urban clouds. The reported results provide new kinetic data for the •OH reaction with highly oxygenated molecules, thereby facilitating the development of SARs and atmospheric models.

item.title: Coupled Mechanisms of Surrounding Rock Stability and Spontaneous Combustion Control in Gob-Side Entry Retaining under Fully Mechanized Top Coal Caving
item.description:
Abstract
The safety of gob-side entry retaining (GER) in fully mechanized top coal caving (FMTC) panels involves the interacting evolution of surrounding rock deformation, roadside backfill body (RBB) damage, air leakage, oxygen migration, and residual coal oxidation. However, the mechanical origin of leakage channel formation and its connection with spontaneous combustion risk remain insufficiently clarified. This study investigates the 090515 working face of Duanwang Coal Mine and develops a fracture-mediated framework linking top coal–RBB load transfer, RBB damage evolution, goaf air leakage, oxygen distribution, and carbon monoxide (CO) response. An analytical load-transfer model was established to clarify the role of top coal in the local bearing system, while three-dimensional discrete-element simulation was used to examine RBB fracture development and structural degradation. Sulfur hexafluoride (SF6) tracer tests were conducted to quantify the spatial attenuation of goaf air leakage, and laboratory oxidation tests and field gas monitoring were used to identify the site-specific oxidation-prone zone. The results indicate that insufficient top coal stiffness and progressive RBB damage are associated with deterioration of the local bearing and sealing system, while stronger leakage is observed in the near-face region. The measured SF6-derived apparent leakage velocity decreases with distance from the working face, allowing the leakage field to be divided into a high-variability zone, a transitional-attenuation zone, and a relatively stable low-velocity zone. Based on closed oxygen consumption tests and field gas monitoring, the 12–18% oxygen concentration range was adopted as a site-specific criterion for identifying the oxidation-prone zone in the 090515 goaf. Field application indicates that the integrated control strategy was associated with reduced roadway deformation and a short-term decrease in CO concentration during the available monitoring period. The findings provide a field-supported basis for coordinated control of surrounding rock stability and spontaneous combustion risk in FMTC conditions with GER.

item.title: Nanoarchitectonics-Enabled Multifunctional Hydrogel with Artesunate-Loaded Mesoporous Silica Nanoparticles for Accelerated Diabetic Wound Healing via JAK1/STAT3-Mediated Macrophage Reprogramming
item.description:
Abstract
Diabetic wound healing is critically hindered by persistent macrophage dysfunction, characterized by an inability to transition from the pro-inflammatory M1 to the pro-healing M2 phenotype. Artesunate (ART) holds therapeutic promise for immunomodulation, yet its clinical translation is constrained by poor aqueous solubility and lack of sustained local delivery. Inspired by the concept of nanoarchitectonics, a post-nanotechnology paradigm that constructs functional material systems through the deliberate orchestration of atoms, molecules, and nanomaterials, we herein architect a multifunctional composite hydrogel (TA/CMCS/OSA/MSN@ART) via an integrated multi-step assembly strategy. This nanoarchitectonic design hierarchically integrates molecular building blocks, carboxymethyl chitosan, oxidized sodium alginate, and tannic acid, through Schiff-base dynamic covalent crosslinking and supramolecular hydrogen bonding, while simultaneously embedding ART-loaded mesoporous silica nanoparticles (MSN@ART) as functional nanoscale units within the porous scaffold. This hydrogel demonstrates favorable physicochemical characteristics and exhibits notable biological properties, including low hemolysis, potent antibacterial and antioxidant activities, and high biocompatibility. Importantly, the ART-loaded hydrogel significantly accelerates diabetic wound healing by facilitating macrophage polarization toward the M2 phenotype. This effect appears to be closely associated with the activation of the JAK1/STAT3 signaling pathway. These findings establish nanoarchitectonics as a powerful and versatile methodology for designing advanced biomaterials, offering a transformative strategy for the management of chronic diabetic wounds.

item.title: Branched Poly- l -Lysine Molecules for the Delivery of Nucleic Acids
item.description:
Abstract
Gene therapy is a rapidly expanding area of research, with a growing number of publications and clinical trials since the advent of the field. Despite substantial advances, one of the most significant roadblocks faced during gene therapy is the failure to efficiently deliver genetic material into target cells at levels sufficient to achieve a therapeutic effect. Therefore, an active and crucial area of research is the development of gene therapy platforms that can efficiently and safely transfect cells with low levels of cytotoxicity and immunogenicity. Toward this, cationic polymers offer a desirable platform due to their ability to self-complex with genetic material, ability to transfect cells, their ease and controllability of production, and their low immunogenicity. Though cationic polymers can induce some level of toxicity due to their positive charge and, display lower transfection efficacy compared to virus-based gene transfection agents, alterations can be made to the polymers (i.e., charge, molecular architecture, molecular weight, etc.) to help increase their transfection efficiency and mitigate drawbacks. In this study, we explored such alterations with a cationic polymer, branched poly-l-lysine (BPL), with lysine as the repeating unit, for their ability to transfect cells using plasmid DNA (pDNA) as genetic material.

item.title: A Label-Free Method to Quantify Early Stage Amyloid Aggregation via Intrinsic Phenylalanine Fluorescence
item.description:
Abstract
The aggregation of amyloid-forming peptides is a dynamic, complex process that underlies their diverse biological activities, from physiological functions to disease-associated dysfunctions. While the structure of fibrillar end-products is well-characterized for most amyloids, the heterogeneous and often transient oligomers, likely key in cytotoxicity, remain poorly investigated, especially for peptides with low-yield aromatic residues. Here, by exploiting and developing flow induced dispersion analysis in both peak and front modes, we demonstrate that intrinsic phenylalanine fluorescence can be harnessed to quantify the conversion of diffusing monomers into nondiffusing oligomers and fibrils. This approach is validated using PSMα3, a tryptophan- and tyrosine-free peptide from S. aureus, known for its fast amyloid fibrillation and key roles in bacterial virulence. We indeed characterize its low-molecular-weight oligomers, and size evolution from 2 to 10 nm over time. Importantly, to further validate the robustness of our front-mode approach, we apply it to hIAPP, a tyrosine-containing, tryptophan-free peptide, with critical outcome in type 2 diabetes. Our results overcome the limitations of traditional biochemical and biophysical amyloid assays by extending analysis from large oligomers and fibrils to small heterogeneous oligomers, under near-physiological conditions. This study thus offers a new analytical framework, thereby filling a critical gap in amyloid research, to probe the early stages of aggregation, key in the design of alternative therapeutics for amyloid-diseases.

item.title: DFT Study of NH 3 Adsorption and Decomposition on Zr(0001)
item.description:
Abstract
Ammonia adsorption and decomposition to hydrogen and nitrogen is studied on the Zr(0001) surface using density functional theory within the generalized gradient approximation and a supercell approach at a coverage of 0.25 ML. Different adsorption sites are considered for NH3 and its dehydrogenated species. We find that ammonia adsorbs readily and decomposes to atomic nitrogen and hydrogen through an exothermic pathway with relatively small kinetic barriers. The NH decomposition step is identified as rate-limiting. Nitrogen strongly favors subsurface incorporation over surface adsorption, whereas hydrogen remains on the surface. The reaction energetics and kinetic barriers obtained in this work are compared with previous studies of NH3 adsorption and decomposition via sequential hydrogen abstraction on ZrB2(0001).

item.title: Dependent Morphological Transformation of Sc-MOFs with Boosted Catalytic Performance
item.description:
Abstract
The coordination modulation method of metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) is intensively researched for creating new materials with highly controlled particle size and morphology because these factors strongly influence the abilities of gas separation, adsorption, and catalysis. Most of the research focuses on the ratio of modulators and the type of reagent. However, this approach does not necessarily optimize the structures, which reduces the potential of the materials. In this study, we investigated the effect of reaction time on the particle morphologies and revealed the mechanism of morphological changes from dodecahedron structures to flower-like structures. According to more detailed studies, this was attributed to the amount of acetic acid, the formation of sheet-like structures, and aggregation. Furthermore, flower-like structures have higher catalytic performance than dodecahedron-like structures. In addition, flower-like structures displayed a type IV adsorption isotherm unlike dodecahedron-like structures displaying type I. Therefore, this approach based on reaction time and the mechanism could lead to new MOFs with outstanding properties.

item.title: Optimization of Sensor Response Time in Microfluidics-Based Biosensors with Balanced Analyte Transport
item.description:
Abstract
The combined effect of geometric obstruction and auxiliary inlet on sensor response time for a microfluidics-integrated biosensor has been numerically investigated in this study. The flow behavior and mass transfer of an analyte have been modeled using incompressible Navier–Stokes equations coupled with convection–diffusion and Langmuir adsorption kinetics equations for comparable time scales of diffusion and surface reaction. Introduction of a block increases the analyte velocity near the sensor surface with subsequent reduction in diffusion boundary layer thickness, thereby ameliorating the sensor response time. Insertion of an auxiliary inlet diminishes the sensor response time to a greater extent by confining a thin layer of analyte above the sensor surface. A systematic parametric study is conducted to evaluate the blended effects of block height, block position, block width, auxiliary inlet position, and auxiliary inlet velocity on sensor performance. Taguchi-based optimization techniques employing an L27 orthogonal array alongside signal-to-noise ratio analysis and analysis of variance have been utilized for identification of optimal parameter combinations. The results indicate that the auxiliary inlet velocity is the most influential parameter with a contribution of 65.8% toward the decrement in sensor response time. The findings demonstrate that the combination of block-induced flow-field modifications and auxiliary-inlet-mediated flow confinement effect significantly augments analyte transport to the sensor surface, thereby decreasing the sensor response time by approximately 92% in comparison to the scenario devoid of a block and auxiliary inlet. This study provides valuable insights for the design and optimization of point-of-care microfluidic devices with reduced detection time.

item.title: Experimental Study on the Seepage Characteristics of Rough Single Fracture in Limestone under Stress–Seepage Pressure Condition
item.description:
Abstract
